title: Late Suburban Currents
statement: The vernacular photographers of the early twenty-first century, working almost entirely from the telephone in their pocket, paved the way for an emerging coterie of image makers who wished to push the limits of documentation beyond the merely useful. They endeavored to infuse the ordinary with a transcendent spirit, photographing what was in front of them before it went cold, flew away or was thrown out.

Between 2019 and 2026 the artist moved between New York and Chicago, and the work moves with them: from the warm, orange-leaning light of the early pictures to the cooler blues of a window in March, and finally to a screen glowing at 11:58 p.m. Recurring subjects include beverages, sky and evidence of purchase. This exhibition, like many before it, may assign more intention to a receipt than a receipt can bear.

Drawn from the artist's camera roll, *Late Suburban Currents* explores a dynamic period of interchange between the planned and the accidental, when an artist once again tested the possibilities of pointing a phone at something and pressing the button.

works.title: Study for a Parking Lot
works.label:
Made on the longest day of the year, this early work finds the artist already at ease with the grand subject of the American evening. A sun the color of apricot sinks behind a single streetlight, which stands in for the vertical figure of classical landscape. The painted lines of the lot recede toward the horizon with a confidence Renaissance perspective would recognize.

Nobody, it should be said, was parking.

The picture belongs to a long American conversation about the empty lot and the open road. In the 1960s Ed Ruscha photographed Los Angeles parking lots from the air and published them as a book, treating the most overlooked spaces of the city as worthy of a catalogue. The artist comes down to ground level and adds a sunset, which Ruscha would never have allowed.

The tonal range is remarkable for a phone of its generation: apricot at the top, violet at the horizon, the asphalt a deep slate. It is the earliest dated work in the collection, and it sets out a theme the artist will return to for years: beauty in places designed for something else.
works.film_line: A sun the color of apricot, a single streetlight, and nobody parking.
works.alt: An orange and purple sunset over an empty parking lot with one streetlight.

works.title: Self Portrait as a Cold Coffee
works.label:
A cup, still full, photographed at 8:12 a.m. and never finished. The artist centers it with the confidence of a still life painter, letting the warm browns of the counter rise around it like a frame. Made in the first autumn of what the chronology calls the Early Period, it is one of several works in which the artist documents a plan rather than an event. The coffee was meant to be drunk. The picture was taken instead.

The overhead view belongs to the tradition of the still life, which since the Dutch painters of the 1600s has asked ordinary objects on tables to stand in for larger ideas about time and appetite. Those painters favored the half eaten pie and the overturned glass, reminders that pleasure does not last. The artist goes further, and photographs the meal before it has begun.

The work anticipates a whole genre of the decade, the picture taken instead of the thing itself. It is, in that sense, a self portrait: not of the artist's face, but of their mornings.
works.film_line: The coffee was meant to be drunk. The picture was taken instead.
works.alt: A full cup of coffee seen from above on a brown counter.

works.title: Window, Chicago (March)
works.label:
The artist's arrival in Chicago is announced by a change of palette. The orange of the New York years gives way to a pale, uncertain blue, divided by the dark cross of a window frame into four equal skies. Clouds drift across each pane as if unaware of the grid imposed on them. Critics have read the work as a meditation on staying inside. The artist has not commented, possibly because they were inside.

The grid has been one of the great forms of modern art, from Piet Mondrian's black lines to the window paintings of the Romantics, who loved to stand indoors and look out. Caspar David Friedrich painted his own studio window in the early 1800s as a frame between the known and the unknown. Here the unknown is Chicago in March.

The new camera, a Pixel 6, renders the blues cool and even, and the softness of the clouds suggests a faint fog on the glass. The window frame itself is nearly black, so that each pane becomes its own small painting. Four skies, one afternoon, no plans.
works.alt: A blue sky with small clouds seen through a dark window frame divided into four panes.

works.title: Untitled (Receipt)
works.label:
A slip of thermal paper floats on a dark ground, slightly askew, its lines of type softened into pure rhythm. Long dismissed as a document, the receipt is here returned to its true condition as an abstract composition of horizontal bands. Whether it was photographed for a reimbursement, a return or a dispute, the archive does not say. The museum chooses to believe it was for this.

The receipt joins a long line of everyday paper elevated by artists: the newspaper scraps glued into Cubist collages by Picasso and Braque from 1912, the tickets and wrappers of Kurt Schwitters, the bills and forms of conceptual art in the 1960s. What those artists did with glue and scissors, the artist accomplishes with a single photograph taken at lunchtime.

The composition is deliberately off balance. The slip leans to the right, its top edge clipped, and the dark ground swallows the corners. Read as abstraction, it is a study in horizontal rhythm. Read as a document, it is illegible. The work refuses to choose.
works.alt: A white paper receipt with lines of faint print, lying at an angle on a dark surface.

works.title: Composition with Blue Notification
works.medium: Screenshot, found digital material, captured at 11:58 p.m.
works.label:
Two minutes before midnight, the artist abandons the camera entirely and turns to the screen itself. Rounded grey and blue forms stack in a strict vertical order that recalls Mondrian by way of a group chat. The text has been lost to time and to the curator's discretion. What remains is the shape of a conversation, and the late hour, which says enough.

In 1917 Marcel Duchamp submitted a factory made urinal to an exhibition and called it *Fountain*, arguing that the choice of an object could be an artistic act. The screenshot is the readymade of the phone era: nothing is made, everything is chosen. The artist presses two buttons at once and the moment is kept.

The Screenshot Period, as the chronology calls it, is the least understood in the artist's career, partly because so much of its material is private. This work survives because its content has faded into pure shape, which is how most conversations are remembered anyway.
works.alt: A phone screenshot of alternating blue and grey rounded message bubbles.

works.title: Pigeon, Possibly
works.label:
The most recent work in the collection is also its most contested. A grey form, softened almost to vapor, holds still for exactly as long as the shutter needs and not a moment longer. Its orange eye is the only point of focus in the picture. Scholars agree it is a bird. Beyond that, consensus collapses. In the artist's late style, the subject is less important than the attempt.

Blur has a distinguished history. Around 1900 the Pictorialists chose soft focus on purpose, believing it made photography more like painting. Later, Gerhard Richter blurred his paintings of photographs until they looked like half remembered things. The artist joins this tradition with a subject that simply would not hold still.

The palette is almost entirely grey, warmed only by the eye and a faint brown at the edges. The newest camera in the collection, an iPhone 15, has done its best. The bird has done its best too. What remains is the record of two parties trying, which may be all a photograph ever is.
works.film_line: Scholars agree it is a bird. Beyond that, consensus collapses.
works.alt: A very blurry grey bird, probably a pigeon, against a grey background.

entries.heading: Early Period: New York
entries.text: The artist's first surviving works are made in New York on an iPhone 8. Warm light, empty lots and unfinished beverages establish the concerns of a lifetime.
entries.room_text: The artist's first surviving works were made in New York in 2019, on an iPhone 8. They are warm, centered and quietly ambitious: a sunset over an empty lot, a coffee from above. Look for the orange light that runs through this room, and for the artist's early habit of photographing things just before they happen.

entries.heading: The Chicago Years
entries.text: A move west brings a cooler palette and a new camera. The artist begins to photograph paperwork. Scholars disagree on whether this was a phase.
entries.room_text: A move west brought a new camera and a cooler palette. The works in this room are blue and grey, shot through windows and at tables, and for the first time the artist turns to paper and documents. Scholars disagree on whether this was a phase. Look for the grids.

entries.heading: The Screenshot Period
entries.text: The camera is set aside for the screen. Work from this period is made almost exclusively after 11 p.m.
entries.room_text: For a time the camera was set aside entirely in favour of the screen. Work from this period is made almost exclusively after 11 p.m., and most of it is not on view, for reasons the museum respects.

entries.heading: Late Style
entries.text: Back in New York, the artist returns to the street and to the bird. The work grows looser, faster and harder to identify.
entries.room_text: Back in New York, the artist returns to the street and to the bird. The work grows looser, faster and harder to identify. Critics call it a return to form, or possibly a return to forms.

visitor_note: You do not have to read everything. Look at what you like. Get what you get.
